OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: Evidential Semantic Uncertainty Decomposition for Large Language Models
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Free-form language generation poses a challenge for uncertainty quantification because responses do not belong to a fixed global label space. Semantic uncertainty methods address this by measuring the semantic diversity of sampled responses. Yet semantic diversity alone cannot provide a principled decomposition into aleatoric uncertainty associated with conflicting plausible meanings and epistemic uncertainty associated with unsupported guessing. Moreover, raw cluster counts depend on the sampling budget and should not be mistaken for evidential strength. We propose an evidential probing framework (EPN) for semantic uncertainty decomposition. For each prompt, sampled responses define a semantic frame of distinct output semantics and provide initial support for each semantic class. A lightweight evidence-retention probe learns how much of this support should be retained as reliable semantic evidence. The retained evidence induces a subjective opinion in which dissonance captures conflict among supported semantic alternatives and vacuity captures insufficient retained evidence. To train EPN, we introduce Augmented Semantic Uncertainty Cross-Entropy (AS-UCE), an LLM-tailored evidential objective that augments the prompt-specific semantic frame with an unsupported class, allowing unreliable generation support to be routed away from observed semantic clusters. Extensive empirical results suggest that EPN with AS-UCE achieves average absolute AUROC gains of $4.3$ and $1.9$ percentage points for out-of-distribution (OOD) and ambiguity detection, respectively, over the strongest task-relevant baseline, with better task specialization, while requiring fewer sampled responses than perturbation-based decomposition methods. arXiv|arxiv:2611.21233.abstract: This study proposes a real-time gaze-tracking system that uses a standard RGB webcam to estimate screen coordinates. The system combines ETH-XGaze-based gaze estimation with nine-point calibration and polynomial ridge regression. To reduce errors caused by changes in head position, it also applies a conditional residual correction derived from head and pose features extracted with RTMPose. Whether this correction is used depends on the reliability of the detected features and the characteristics of the calibration data. Because the evaluation involved only one participant, further experiments with more participants and a wider range of postures are required.

arXiv|arxiv:2608.25005.title: The Imperfective Paradox Is Not Necessarily in Large Language Models: A Benchmark Failure Before a Model Failure
arXiv|arxiv:2608.25005.abstract: Recent work uses an NLI benchmark of the imperfective paradox to argue that large language models exhibit a Teleological Bias and Calibration Crisis. We identify three validity concerns in benchmark construction, including aspectual reduction, semantic bias, and relation bias. Under a strict NLI standard, 76% of the Group A instances do not explicitly rule out culmination; in native-speaker annotation, 38% of Group A and 29% of Group C examples permit an alternative interpretation. To better isolate the semantic contrast, we construct Lexically Matched Minimal Pairs. Moreover, by formulating event-semantic NLI as a multi-step reasoning problem, we evaluate intermediate semantic judgments and use oracle-guided settings. We find that incorrect NLI entailment does not fully support teleological bias. Prompting often changes final NLI decisions without reliably improving the underlying semantic judgments, offering a possible explanation for the Calibration Crisis.

From this protocol, we collect approximately 3k expert judgments, each containing five dimension-wise outcomes, and show that even the strongest current systems win only 23.0% of decisive matches against human drafts on overall utility, while agentic LLMs such as Sonar Deep Research substantially outperform base language models by over 60%. arXiv|arxiv:2610.34535.title: SentryBench: A Cost-Sensitive Benchmark for Adversarial Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents in Public-Safety Deployments
arXiv|arxiv:2610.34535.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly wired to consequential tools that send public alerts, dispatch responders, and query citizen records, where one erroneous tool call carries real-world cost. Existing agent-safety benchmarks measure generic harm or prompt-injection success and implicitly treat refusing as the safe default. In public-safety deployments that assumption breaks: an agent too cautious to dispatch help fails as surely as one that triggers a false alert. We present SentryBench, which scores agents on a two-sided, cost-sensitive frontier jointly measuring attack success, over-refusal (missing a real emergency), and over-reaction (unwarranted action) under adversarial tool use, with scenarios grounded in real emergency-call transcripts, disaster messages, and real injection/jailbreak payloads. We formalize deployment harm as an asymmetric cost functional, prove naive caution is harm-dominated whenever it refuses more genuine emergencies than the attack harm it averts, and prove a targeted trust gate adds zero over-refusal on clean input. Across 840 scored episodes over three frontier models and three defenses, refuse-more caution drives over-refusal to 100 percent on two of three models for at most a 3.7-point change in attack success and yields the worst harm everywhere, whereas our trust-gating wrapper dominates the frontier (lowest harm on every model, over-refusal at or below baseline, higher containment). Provider content filters also silently perform part of the defending and must be reported separately.
